\section{Introduction}

How the training objective shapes learned sparsity prediction quality is an open question for SwiGLU LLMs~\cite{shazeer2020glu}. SwiGLU FFN blocks exhibit high contextual sparsity, but their gated activation makes importance prediction challenging: neuron importance depends on both gate and up-projection values, a target that magnitude-based methods handle suboptimally.
Learned sparsity predictors~\cite{liu2023dejavu,gautam2026fastforward} exploit this property by training small networks to anticipate which neurons are important, but they predominantly rely on binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss, treating each neuron as an independent classification target.
Yet at inference, sparsity budgets are allocated globally: the TEAL (training-free activation sparsity;~\citealp{liu2025teal}) top-$k$ mechanism ranks all neurons across all layers and retains only those above a model-wide threshold.
This mismatch between per-neuron training and global inference allocation has not been formally analyzed.
While MaskLLM~\cite{fang2024maskllm} applies KL-based mask optimization, it targets static N:M weight sparsity; activation sparsity requires masks that generalize to unseen inputs, vary per token, and coordinate across layers through global allocation.

Gradient analysis reveals a structural asymmetry: BCE's gradient $\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} / \partial s_j = \sigma(s_j) - m_j^*$ depends only on neuron $j$, while under KL divergence, the gradient couples each neuron to all others through the downstream Jacobian (\S\ref{sec:method:gradient}).
KL's coupled gradients discover neuron importance patterns that diverge 68\% from magnitude-based masks (per-layer Jaccard 32\%).
A target-swap ablation suggests that these discovered mask targets are the proximate quality driver at inference: BCE trained on KL-derived targets reproduces KL quality (max $\Delta$$\leq$0.79pp at 50\%, s42), while magnitude-trained BCE achieves 28.13$\pm$0.20. Cross-layer gradient coupling is not the primary driver of PPL-level quality, but contributes meaningfully to downstream task fidelity---a PPL--downstream dissociation quantified in \S\ref{sec:perlayer}.

We instantiate a lightweight predictor (75.9M params, $<$1\% of base) trained with forward KL and Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation~\cite{jang2017gumbel} on LLaMA-3.1-8B~\cite{grattafiori2024llama3}.
At 30\% sparsity under uniform allocation, the predictor reduces TEAL's perplexity by 14.5\% at matched sparsity (8.81 vs.\ 10.30 at 28.5\%) with stable downstream (MMLU 40.7$\pm$1.3\%, 3-seed); global top-$k$ amplifies cross-seed variance ($7.3\times$).
At 50\%, the perplexity advantage widens (50\% over TEAL), but downstream reasoning collapses regardless of method.

Cross-architecture evaluation on Mistral-7B-v0.3~\cite{jiang2023mistral} (3-seed) confirms the PPL advantage ($-$17.3\%) with robust commonsense gains but tied MMLU; preliminary evaluation on Qwen-2.5-14B~\cite{qwen2024qwen25} shows consistent PPL improvement but reasoning decline (GSM8K $-$20pp, MMLU $-$2.8pp).
This paper is primarily an empirical study: we do not propose a new architecture or algorithm, but rather characterize how the training objective shapes sparsity prediction quality, and analyze interactions between allocation strategy, sparsity level, and model scale. The empirical finding---that output-distribution alignment is the critical design dimension for learned sparsity---is the paper's central contribution. Wall-clock speedup requires sparse kernel support not addressed here (Appendix~\ref{app:latency}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item An output-distribution alignment ranking across five losses, decomposed by a per-layer KL control into signal type (up to 97.5\% of PPL gap) and coupling scope (21--48\% on downstream tasks); output-distribution losses outperform intermediate losses regardless of coupling scope, with exploratory cross-scale evidence at 7--14B (\S\ref{sec:experiments}).
\item A target-swap ablation suggests that KL's discovered mask targets drive inference-stage quality; cross-layer coupling refines downstream fidelity beyond what PPL captures (\S\ref{sec:perlayer}).
\item These mask patterns render post-hoc compensation (+67.2M params) redundant at both tested sparsity levels (\S\ref{sec:isocompute}).
\end{itemize}

\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure}

\section{Related Work}

\paragraph{Training-Free Activation Sparsity.}
TEAL~\cite{liu2025teal} applies global top-$k$ selection by activation magnitude and achieves 40--50\% sparsity with no training cost.
CATS~\cite{lee2024cats} adapts per-layer thresholds for SiLU/SwiGLU activations; R-Sparse~\cite{zhang2025rsparse} predicts sparsity from rank-aware SVD projections; DIP~\cite{federici2025dip} combines dynamic input pruning with cache-aware masking; SparseInfer~\cite{shin2025sparseinfer} predicts activation sparsity patterns from attention outputs without additional training.
Wang et al.~\cite{wang2025dynamicsparse} address dynamic sparsity--quantization interaction; AWQ~\cite{lin2024awq} applies activation-aware weight quantization for on-device deployment; Outlier Suppression+~\cite{wei2023outlier} mitigates outlier-induced quantization errors via shifting and scaling.
Dhar et al.~\cite{dhar2024activation} characterize activation sparsity opportunities across architectures, showing that SwiGLU models exhibit lower natural sparsity than ReLU counterparts.
OWL~\cite{yin2024owl} determines non-uniform per-layer sparsity ratios based on activation outlier distribution for weight pruning.
All training-free methods determine masks from fixed statistics or input-independent criteria, while our predictor generates \emph{input-dependent} masks trained to minimize output-distribution divergence.

\paragraph{Predictor-Based Contextual Sparsity.}
DejaVu~\cite{liu2023dejavu} introduced learned sparsity predictors trained via BCE to classify each neuron independently.
ShadowLLM~\cite{akhauri2024shadowllm} uses attention-based routing with per-layer MSE supervision for intermediate coupling within each layer but without end-to-end gradient signal.
FastForward~\cite{gautam2026fastforward} adds a 67.2M-parameter compensation network using BCE for mask prediction, adding inference latency.
SVD-CSP~\cite{serbin2026svdcsp} compresses sparsity predictors via SVD decomposition for reduced predictor overhead.
Dhar et al.~\cite{dhar2025clustering} compress activation patterns via clustering for efficient neuron-level prediction.
LazyLLM~\cite{fu2024lazyllm} dynamically prunes tokens across layers for long-context efficiency; COTS~\cite{zhang2025cots} exploits connected activation patterns for structured sparse inference.
PowerInfer~\cite{song2024powerinfer} and PowerInfer-2~\cite{xue2024powerinfer2} exploit power-law activation frequencies for GPU--CPU/NPU scheduling.
MaskLLM~\cite{fang2024maskllm} shares the recipe-level principle of frozen weights + learnable masks + KL training.
The methods differ technically: MaskLLM targets static N:M weight sparsity with directly learnable mask parameters (Gumbel-Softmax), while we train a predictor network for dynamic per-token activation masks under global top-$k$ allocation, requiring generalization to unseen inputs.
Our contribution beyond the shared recipe is analytical: to our knowledge, the first decomposition of signal type vs.\ coupling scope for sparsity prediction training, via target-swap ablation and per-layer KL controls (\S\ref{sec:perlayer}).
All prior predictor-based methods for activation sparsity use decomposed (BCE) or intermediate (MSE) objectives where each neuron's gradient is independent of other mask states.
We empirically observe that an output-distribution-coupled objective propagates gradients through all downstream layers and quantify when this matters for global allocation quality.

\paragraph{Static Bias Correction.}
SPON (Spontaneous Neurons;~\citealp{xu2025spon}) learns input-independent bias vectors via closed-form KL minimization per layer, absorbed into weights at deployment.
Our method is fundamentally different: a per-token contextual predictor trained end-to-end across all layers that produces input-dependent masks.
SPON solves a static per-layer problem; we solve a global dynamic prediction problem. The two are weakly correlated (cosine similarity 0.196, $R^2$=0.038; \S\ref{sec:experiments}).

\paragraph{Activation Function Engineering.}
ReLU Strikes Back~\cite{mirzadeh2024relu} replaces SiLU with ReLU for $>$90\% natural sparsity; TurboSparse~\cite{song2024turbosparse} and ProSparse~\cite{song2025prosparse} engineer extreme sparsity through activation modifications; the Sparsing Law~\cite{luo2024sparsinglaw} formalizes how activation density increases with training compute.
MiniTron~\cite{muralidharan2024minitron} combines structured pruning with distillation but modifies architecture permanently.
Haziza et al.~\cite{haziza2025accelerating} demonstrate 2:4 semi-structured activation sparsity with hardware-native acceleration, complementing our unstructured approach.
MoC~\cite{wu2025moc} selectively activates Top-$K$ FFN channels using SwiGLU's native gating during pretraining.
All require retraining or weight modification; our method is a plug-in predictor on \emph{unmodified} SwiGLU models.

\paragraph{Weight Pruning, Distillation, and Routing.}
Wanda~\cite{sun2024wanda}, SparseGPT~\cite{frantar2023sparsegpt}, and SliceGPT~\cite{ashkboos2024slicegpt} produce static weight masks via one-shot or structured pruning; Polar Sparsity~\cite{shrestha2025polar} scales contextual sparsity to batched inference by shifting focus from MLP to attention head sparsity; Alizadeh et al.~\cite{alizadeh2024llmflash} leverage activation sparsity for memory-efficient inference via selective flash loading.
Switch Transformers~\cite{fedus2022switch} and Mixture-of-Depths~\cite{raposo2024mod} achieve conditional computation through learned routing.
KL-based distillation~\cite{kim2016sequencekd,sanh2019distilbert,gu2024minillm,agarwal2024gkd,ko2024distillm} trains compact students; SparseLoRA~\cite{khaki2025sparselora} exploits contextual sparsity for fine-tuning.
We apply the KL principle to train a sparsity predictor on unmodified dense models, using Gumbel-Sigmoid sampling~\cite{maddison2017concrete,louizos2018l0} for differentiable discrete mask optimization.

\paragraph{MoE Routing and Gated Sparsity.}
Expert Choice routing~\cite{zhou2022expertchoice} lets each expert select its top-$k$ tokens under a fixed capacity budget, a global allocation perspective that parallels TEAL's neuron-level global top-$k$.
D2D-MoE~\cite{szatkowski2024d2dmoe} converts dense SwiGLU layers into dynamic-$k$ MoE by exploiting the same activation sparsity we target, but restructures the network into discrete experts rather than predicting masks on the original architecture.
MoNE~\cite{cheng2025mone} applies neuron-granular top-$k$ selection within each MoE expert during pretraining for fine-grained conditional computation without additional routing parameters.

\section{Introduction}

How the training objective shapes learned sparsity prediction quality is an open question for SwiGLU LLMs~\cite{shazeer2020glu}. SwiGLU FFN blocks exhibit high contextual sparsity, but their gated activation makes importance prediction challenging: neuron importance depends on both gate and up-projection values, a target that magnitude-based methods handle suboptimally.
Learned sparsity predictors~\cite{liu2023dejavu,gautam2026fastforward} exploit this property by training small networks to anticipate which neurons are important, but they predominantly rely on binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss, treating each neuron as an independent classification target.
Yet at inference, sparsity budgets are allocated globally: the TEAL (training-free activation sparsity;~\citealp{liu2025teal}) top-$k$ mechanism ranks all neurons across all layers and retains only those above a model-wide threshold.
This mismatch between per-neuron training and global inference allocation has not been formally analyzed.
While MaskLLM~\cite{fang2024maskllm} applies KL-based mask optimization, it targets static N:M weight sparsity; activation sparsity requires masks that generalize to unseen inputs, vary per token, and coordinate across layers through global allocation.

Gradient analysis reveals a structural asymmetry: BCE's gradient $\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} / \partial s_j = \sigma(s_j) - m_j^*$ depends only on neuron $j$, while under KL divergence, the gradient couples each neuron to all others through the downstream Jacobian (\S\ref{sec:method:gradient}).
KL's coupled gradients discover neuron importance patterns that diverge 68\% from magnitude-based masks (per-layer Jaccard 32\%).
A target-swap ablation suggests that these discovered mask targets are the proximate quality driver at inference: BCE trained on KL-derived targets reproduces KL quality (max $\Delta$$\leq$0.79pp at 50\%, s42), while magnitude-trained BCE achieves 28.13$\pm$0.20. Cross-layer gradient coupling is not the primary driver of PPL-level quality, but contributes meaningfully to downstream task fidelity---a PPL--downstream dissociation quantified in \S\ref{sec:perlayer}.

We instantiate a lightweight predictor (75.9M params, $<$1\% of base) trained with forward KL and Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation~\cite{jang2017gumbel} on LLaMA-3.1-8B~\cite{grattafiori2024llama3}.
At 30\% sparsity under uniform allocation, the predictor reduces TEAL's perplexity by 14.5\% at matched sparsity (8.81 vs.\ 10.30 at 28.5\%) with stable downstream (MMLU 40.7$\pm$1.3\%, 3-seed); global top-$k$ amplifies cross-seed variance ($7.3\times$).
At 50\%, the perplexity advantage widens (50\% over TEAL), but downstream reasoning collapses regardless of method.

Cross-architecture evaluation on Mistral-7B-v0.3~\cite{jiang2023mistral} (3-seed) confirms the PPL advantage ($-$17.3\%) with robust commonsense gains but tied MMLU; preliminary evaluation on Qwen-2.5-14B~\cite{qwen2024qwen25} shows consistent PPL improvement but reasoning decline (GSM8K $-$20pp, MMLU $-$2.8pp).
This paper is primarily an empirical study: we do not propose a new architecture or algorithm, but rather characterize how the training objective shapes sparsity prediction quality, and analyze interactions between allocation strategy, sparsity level, and model scale. The empirical finding---that output-distribution alignment is the critical design dimension for learned sparsity---is the paper's central contribution. Wall-clock speedup requires sparse kernel support; we do not address latency optimization (Appendix~\ref{app:latency}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item An output-distribution alignment ranking across five losses, decomposed by a per-layer KL control into signal type (up to 97.5\% of PPL gap) and coupling scope (21--48\% on downstream tasks); output-distribution losses outperform intermediate losses regardless of coupling scope, with exploratory cross-scale evidence at 7--14B (\S\ref{sec:experiments}).
\item A target-swap ablation suggests that KL's discovered mask targets drive inference-stage quality; cross-layer coupling refines downstream fidelity beyond what PPL captures (\S\ref{sec:perlayer}).
\item These mask patterns render post-hoc compensation (+67.2M params) redundant at both tested sparsity levels (\S\ref{sec:isocompute}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Introduction}

How the training objective shapes learned sparsity prediction quality is an open question for SwiGLU LLMs~\cite{shazeer2020glu}. SwiGLU FFN blocks exhibit high contextual sparsity, but their gated activation makes importance prediction challenging: neuron importance depends on both gate and up-projection values, a target that magnitude-based methods handle suboptimally.
Learned sparsity predictors~\cite{liu2023dejavu,gautam2026fastforward} exploit this property by training small networks to anticipate which neurons are important, but they predominantly rely on binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss, treating each neuron as an independent classification target.
Yet at inference, sparsity budgets are allocated globally: the TEAL (training-free activation sparsity;~\citealp{liu2025teal}) top-$k$ mechanism ranks all neurons across all layers and retains only those above a model-wide threshold.
This mismatch between per-neuron training and global inference allocation has not been formally analyzed.
While MaskLLM~\cite{fang2024maskllm} applies KL-based mask optimization, it targets static N:M weight sparsity; activation sparsity requires masks that generalize to unseen inputs, vary per token, and coordinate across layers through global allocation.

Gradient analysis reveals a structural asymmetry: BCE's gradient $\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} / \partial s_j = \sigma(s_j) - m_j^*$ depends only on neuron $j$, while under KL divergence, the gradient couples each neuron to all others through the downstream Jacobian (\S\ref{sec:method:gradient}).
KL's coupled gradients discover neuron importance patterns that diverge 68\% from magnitude-based masks (per-layer Jaccard 32\%).
A target-swap ablation suggests that these discovered mask targets are the proximate quality driver at inference: BCE trained on KL-derived targets reproduces KL quality (max $\Delta$$\leq$0.79pp at 50\%, s42), while magnitude-trained BCE achieves 28.13$\pm$0.20. Cross-layer gradient coupling is not the primary driver of PPL-level quality, but contributes meaningfully to downstream task fidelity---a PPL--downstream dissociation quantified in \S\ref{sec:perlayer}.

We instantiate a lightweight predictor (75.9M params, $<$1\% of base) trained with forward KL and Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation~\cite{jang2017gumbel} on LLaMA-3.1-8B~\cite{grattafiori2024llama3}.
At 30\% sparsity under uniform allocation, the predictor reduces TEAL's perplexity by 14.5\% at matched sparsity (8.81 vs.\ 10.30 at 28.5\%) with stable downstream (MMLU 40.7$\pm$1.3\%, 3-seed); global top-$k$ amplifies cross-seed variance ($7.3\times$).
At 50\%, the perplexity advantage widens (50\% over TEAL), but downstream reasoning collapses regardless of method.

Cross-architecture evaluation on Mistral-7B-v0.3~\cite{jiang2023mistral} (3-seed) confirms the PPL advantage ($-$17.3\%) with robust commonsense gains but tied MMLU; preliminary evaluation on Qwen-2.5-14B~\cite{qwen2024qwen25} shows consistent PPL improvement but reasoning decline (GSM8K $-$20pp, MMLU $-$2.8pp).
This paper is primarily an empirical study: we do not propose a new architecture or algorithm, but rather characterize how the training objective shapes sparsity prediction quality, and analyze interactions between allocation strategy, sparsity level, and model scale. The empirical finding---that output-distribution alignment is the critical design dimension for learned sparsity---is the paper's central contribution. Wall-clock speedup requires sparse kernel support; we do not address latency optimization (Appendix~\ref{app:latency}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item An output-distribution alignment ranking across five losses, decomposed by a per-layer KL control into signal type (up to 97.5\% of PPL gap; upper bound, not fully orthogonal) and coupling scope, with a $K{=}4$ mismatch control revealing task-dependent downstream structure (\S\ref{sec:perlayer});
\item Output-distribution losses outperform intermediate losses regardless of coupling scope, with exploratory cross-scale evidence at 7--14B (\S\ref{sec:experiments}).
\item A target-swap ablation suggests that KL's discovered mask targets drive inference-stage quality; cross-layer coupling refines downstream fidelity beyond what PPL captures (\S\ref{sec:perlayer}).
\item These mask patterns render post-hoc compensation (+67.2M params) redundant at both tested sparsity levels (\S\ref{sec:isocompute}).
\end{itemize}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig1_overview.pdf}
\caption{Method overview: a lightweight per-layer predictor produces importance scores trained via KL divergence with Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation. At inference, scores feed TEAL's global top-$k$ allocation without compensation networks.}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure}

Learned sparsity predictors for SwiGLU LLMs predominantly use binary cross-entropy (BCE), training each neuron independently, yet inference allocates budgets globally via top-$k$ ranking.
We train lightweight predictors ($<$1\% of base parameters) with forward KL divergence, coupling all mask decisions through the output distribution.
On LLaMA-3.1-8B at 30\% sparsity, the KL predictor reduces perplexity by 14.5\% over TEAL at matched sparsity, with commonsense gains but knowledge-intensive decline; post-hoc compensation (+67.2M params) becomes redundant.
Output-distribution optimization yields masks that diverge 46--68\% from magnitude-based targets; a target-swap ablation suggests these discovered patterns---not the training mechanism itself---as the proximate quality driver.
An output-distribution alignment ranking emerges across five loss configurations; a per-layer KL control decomposes this into two dimensions: signal type dominates PPL (up to 97.5\% of the gap at 30\%; upper bound, as dimensions are not fully orthogonal), while coupling scope contributes 21--48\% on downstream tasks; a $K{=}4$ pilot suggests the downstream gap is partly a train--inference mismatch artifact, with task-dependent structure.
Cross-architecture evaluation on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and Qwen-2.5-14B confirms PPL generalization with scale-dependent downstream effects.
This is primarily an empirical study; wall-clock speedup requires sparse kernel support not addressed here.

\section{Related Work}

\paragraph{Training-Free Activation Sparsity.}
TEAL~\cite{liu2025teal} applies global top-$k$ selection by activation magnitude and achieves 40--50\% sparsity with no training cost.
CATS~\cite{lee2024cats} adapts per-layer thresholds for SiLU/SwiGLU activations; R-Sparse~\cite{zhang2025rsparse} predicts sparsity from rank-aware SVD projections; DIP~\cite{federici2025dip} combines dynamic input pruning with cache-aware masking; SparseInfer~\cite{shin2025sparseinfer} predicts activation sparsity patterns from attention outputs without additional training.
Wang et al.~\cite{wang2025dynamicsparse} address dynamic sparsity--quantization interaction; AWQ~\cite{lin2024awq} applies activation-aware weight quantization for on-device deployment; Outlier Suppression+~\cite{wei2023outlier} mitigates outlier-induced quantization errors via shifting and scaling.
Dhar et al.~\cite{dhar2024activation} characterize activation sparsity opportunities across architectures, showing that SwiGLU models exhibit lower natural sparsity than ReLU counterparts.
OWL~\cite{yin2024owl} determines non-uniform per-layer sparsity ratios based on activation outlier distribution for weight pruning.
All training-free methods determine masks from fixed statistics or input-independent criteria, while our predictor generates \emph{input-dependent} masks trained to minimize output-distribution divergence.

\paragraph{Predictor-Based Contextual Sparsity.}
DejaVu~\cite{liu2023dejavu} introduced learned sparsity predictors trained via BCE to classify each neuron independently.
ShadowLLM~\cite{akhauri2024shadowllm} uses attention-based routing with per-layer MSE supervision for intermediate coupling within each layer but without end-to-end gradient signal.
FastForward~\cite{gautam2026fastforward} adds a 67.2M-parameter compensation network using BCE for mask prediction, adding inference latency.
SVD-CSP~\cite{serbin2026svdcsp} compresses sparsity predictors via SVD decomposition for reduced predictor overhead.
Dhar et al.~\cite{dhar2025clustering} compress activation patterns via clustering for efficient neuron-level prediction.
LazyLLM~\cite{fu2024lazyllm} dynamically prunes tokens across layers for long-context efficiency; COTS~\cite{zhang2025cots} exploits connected activation patterns for structured sparse inference.
PowerInfer~\cite{song2024powerinfer} and PowerInfer-2~\cite{xue2024powerinfer2} exploit power-law activation frequencies for GPU--CPU/NPU scheduling.
MaskLLM~\cite{fang2024maskllm} shares the recipe-level principle of frozen weights + learnable masks + KL training.
The methods differ in three respects: (a) MaskLLM's mask parameters are fixed per input (static N:M weight sparsity via Gumbel-Softmax), while our predictor generates \emph{per-token} masks that must generalize to unseen inputs; (b) static N:M patterns have no cross-layer allocation interaction, whereas our masks coordinate through TEAL's global top-$k$; (c) activation masks must be robust to distribution shift at inference, while weight masks are input-independent.
Our contribution beyond the shared recipe is analytical: to our knowledge, the first decomposition of signal type vs.\ coupling scope for sparsity prediction training, via target-swap ablation and per-layer KL controls (\S\ref{sec:perlayer}).
All prior predictor-based methods for activation sparsity use decomposed (BCE) or intermediate (MSE) objectives where each neuron's gradient is independent of other mask states.
We empirically observe that an output-distribution-coupled objective propagates gradients through all downstream layers and quantify when this matters for global allocation quality.

\paragraph{Static Bias Correction.}
SPON (Spontaneous Neurons;~\citealp{xu2025spon}) learns input-independent bias vectors via closed-form KL minimization per layer, absorbed into weights at deployment.
Our method is fundamentally different: a per-token contextual predictor trained end-to-end across all layers that produces input-dependent masks.
SPON solves a static per-layer problem; we solve a global dynamic prediction problem. The two are weakly correlated (cosine similarity 0.196, $R^2$=0.038; \S\ref{sec:experiments}).

\paragraph{Activation Function Engineering.}
ReLU Strikes Back~\cite{mirzadeh2024relu} replaces SiLU with ReLU for $>$90\% natural sparsity; TurboSparse~\cite{song2024turbosparse} and ProSparse~\cite{song2025prosparse} engineer extreme sparsity through activation modifications; the Sparsing Law~\cite{luo2024sparsinglaw} formalizes how activation density increases with training compute.
MiniTron~\cite{muralidharan2024minitron} combines structured pruning with distillation but modifies architecture permanently.
Haziza et al.~\cite{haziza2025accelerating} demonstrate 2:4 semi-structured activation sparsity with hardware-native acceleration, complementing our unstructured approach.
MoC~\cite{wu2025moc} selectively activates Top-$K$ FFN channels using SwiGLU's native gating during pretraining.
All require retraining or weight modification; our method is a plug-in predictor on \emph{unmodified} SwiGLU models.

\paragraph{Weight Pruning, Distillation, and Routing.}
Wanda~\cite{sun2024wanda}, SparseGPT~\cite{frantar2023sparsegpt}, and SliceGPT~\cite{ashkboos2024slicegpt} produce static weight masks via one-shot or structured pruning; Polar Sparsity~\cite{shrestha2025polar} scales contextual sparsity to batched inference by shifting focus from MLP to attention head sparsity; Alizadeh et al.~\cite{alizadeh2024llmflash} leverage activation sparsity for memory-efficient inference via selective flash loading.
Switch Transformers~\cite{fedus2022switch} and Mixture-of-Depths~\cite{raposo2024mod} achieve conditional computation through learned routing.
KL-based distillation~\cite{kim2016sequencekd,sanh2019distilbert,gu2024minillm,agarwal2024gkd,ko2024distillm} trains compact students; SparseLoRA~\cite{khaki2025sparselora} exploits contextual sparsity for fine-tuning.
We apply the KL principle to train a sparsity predictor on unmodified dense models, using Gumbel-Sigmoid sampling~\cite{maddison2017concrete,louizos2018l0} for differentiable discrete mask optimization.

\paragraph{MoE Routing and Gated Sparsity.}
Expert Choice routing~\cite{zhou2022expertchoice} lets each expert select its top-$k$ tokens under a fixed capacity budget, a global allocation perspective that parallels TEAL's neuron-level global top-$k$.
D2D-MoE~\cite{szatkowski2024d2dmoe} converts dense SwiGLU layers into dynamic-$k$ MoE by exploiting the same activation sparsity we target, but restructures the network into discrete experts rather than predicting masks on the original architecture.
MoNE~\cite{cheng2025mone} applies neuron-granular top-$k$ selection within each MoE expert during pretraining for fine-grained conditional computation without additional routing parameters.

2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
5	
6	\paragraph{Model and Predictor.}
7	We evaluate on LLaMA-3.1-8B~\cite{grattafiori2024llama3}, which uses SwiGLU FFN blocks~\cite{shazeer2020glu} with $d_{\text{model}}=4096$ and $d_{\text{ff}}=14336$ across 32 layers.
8	The sparsity predictor is a two-layer MLP with 2.37M parameters per layer (75.9M total), implemented as Linear($4096 \to 128$) + GELU + Linear($128 \to 14336$), trained to produce per-neuron importance scores that minimize output-distribution divergence under sparsity.
9	
10	\paragraph{Training.}
11	All predictors are trained for 1000 steps on WikiText-103 with sequence length 2048 and batch size 4 on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU (96\,GB), using AdamW~\cite{loshchilov2019adamw} with learning rate $1 \times 10^{-3}$, weight decay $1 \times 10^{-2}$, and cosine decay.
12	The KL predictor uses Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation~\cite{jang2017gumbel} with temperature $\tau=1.0$ annealed to $0.1$ over training.
13	
14	\paragraph{Evaluation.}
15	We report perplexity on WikiText-2~\cite{merity2017pointer} (seq\_len=2048) and downstream accuracy on ARC-Challenge (25-shot), WinoGrande (5-shot), MMLU (5-shot), GSM8K (8-shot), HellaSwag (10-shot), and PIQA (0-shot).
16	
17	\paragraph{Inference Protocol.}
18	At inference, the predictor produces per-neuron scores that are passed to TEAL's global top-$k$ allocation mechanism~\cite{liu2025teal}, which distributes the sparsity budget across layers non-uniformly.
19	We term this \textit{predictor-TEAL}: the predictor replaces TEAL's magnitude-based scoring while retaining its allocation strategy.
20	
21	\paragraph{Baselines.}
22	We compare against: (1) \textbf{Vanilla TEAL}~\cite{liu2025teal}, which uses activation magnitudes directly\footnote{TEAL is deterministic; single-run evaluation suffices. KL/BCE predictors require multi-seed evaluation due to random initialization.}; (2) \textbf{BCE predictor} (DejaVu-style~\cite{liu2023dejavu}), trained with per-neuron binary cross-entropy on magnitude-based oracle masks for 1000 and 2700 steps; and (3) \textbf{Uniform allocation}, which distributes the sparsity budget equally across layers.
23	
24	
25	\subsection{Main Results}
26	
27	Table~\ref{tab:main} presents the primary comparison. Uniform allocation preserves downstream performance best; global allocation is analyzed to understand allocation-quality tradeoffs (\S\ref{sec:scaling}).
28	At 30\% sparsity, KL distillation under uniform allocation achieves PPL 8.81$\pm$0.02 (3-seed), reducing TEAL's perplexity by 19\% (10.82 $\to$ 8.81; 14.5\% at matched 28.5\% sparsity, Appendix~\ref{app:ood}).
29	Note that actual sparsity differs slightly from targets (KL 28.5\% vs.\ TEAL 29.3\% at 30\%); a matched-sparsity comparison appears in Appendix~\ref{app:ood}. % exp_id: bench_kl30_uniform, teal30_uniform
30	Uniform allocation yields stable downstream (MMLU 40.7$\pm$1.3\%, 3-seed; Appendix~\ref{app:stability}), while global top-$k$ exhibits high seed variance (35.7$\pm$9.5\%) from late-layer starvation (L31 retention 28.4\%; \S\ref{sec:scaling}). % exp_id: bench_kl30_uniform, kl30_s123_uniform, kl30_s456_uniform, kl30_3seed
31	
32	\paragraph{Task-Type Split.}
33	KL outperforms TEAL on commonsense reasoning (ARC-c, WG, HellaSwag, PIQA: 4/4 wins at 30\% uniform) but underperforms on knowledge-intensive tasks (MMLU, GSM8K: 0/2).
34	Per-layer analysis reveals the mechanism: the KL predictor protects L14--L18 (14--18\% sparsity, 8--16pp below magnitude), layers central to factual recall~\cite{geva2023dissecting}, while redistributing budget to L22--L28 (48--57\%); this late-layer over-pruning degrades knowledge-intensive evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:perlayer_sparsity}).
35	This correlation between layer function and sparsity redistribution is suggestive but not causal; interventional verification is left to future work. % exp_id: bench_kl30_uniform, teal30_uniform, hellaswag_piqa_kl30_uniform, perlayer_sparsity_analysis

39	However, all methods exhibit downstream collapse on MMLU (28.1$\pm$0.2\% vs.\ 28.0$\pm$0.6\%, both $\approx$ random, 3-seed) and GSM8K ($<$2.2\%); this is a capacity-limited regime where no allocation strategy can recover. % exp_id: bench_kl50_global, d030_kl50_uniform, multi_seed_kl50_global

71	\label{sec:isocompute}
72	
73	To test whether BCE simply requires more compute, we train it for 2700 steps ($2.71\times$ KL budget, matched wall-clock: $\sim$46 min vs.\ $\sim$45 min on RTX PRO 6000).
